questions.q: What distinguishes a hyperparameter from a model parameter?
options: A hyperparameter is always a tensor stored inside the model
A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training that gradient descent itself doesn't optimize, like learning rate or batch size
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
A hyperparameter can only take integer values
questions.explain: Model parameters (weights, biases) are learned via gradient descent during training. Hyperparameters, like learning rate or batch size, are chosen beforehand and training cannot adjust them on its own.

questions.q: What does grid search do, as described in this lesson?
options: It samples a fixed number of random configurations
It exhaustively tries every combination of a fixed set of values for each hyperparameter
It trains only one configuration, chosen at random
It adjusts the model architecture automatically without any search
questions.explain: Grid search enumerates every combination across the specified value sets for each hyperparameter, e.g. every (learning rate, batch size) pair from two lists.

questions.q: Why does random search often outperform grid search for the same compute budget?
options: Random search always tests fewer hyperparameters than grid search
Grid search spends a lot of its budget exploring unimportant hyperparameters at full resolution, while random search keeps denser coverage of the important ones even as more are added
Random search never actually trains a model, so it's instant
Grid search cannot use the AdamW optimizer
questions.explain: Because grid search's resolution on each hyperparameter is fixed by the grid, its budget gets diluted across unimportant dimensions. Random sampling tends to keep good coverage of the hyperparameters that actually matter.

questions.q: What does `lr = 10 ** random.uniform(-4, -1)` achieve in the random search example?
options: It samples a batch size uniformly between 10 and -1
It samples a learning rate log-uniformly, giving even coverage across orders of magnitude (e.g. 1e-4 to 1e-1)
It always returns exactly 0.001
It disables the learning rate entirely
questions.explain: Raising 10 to a uniformly sampled exponent produces a log-uniform sample, giving even coverage across orders of magnitude — appropriate since a good learning rate can span several orders of magnitude.

questions.q: What is one common way to reduce the cost of hyperparameter search mentioned in this lesson?
options: Always train every candidate configuration to full convergence before comparing them
Train each candidate for only a few epochs as a cheap proxy, and stop clearly bad trials early instead of letting them run to completion
Skip the validation set entirely and judge candidates by training loss alone
Only ever test one hyperparameter value total
questions.explain: Training every candidate to full convergence is expensive. A common cost-saving approach is using a few epochs as a proxy for final performance and cutting off clearly underperforming trials early.
